div.head: Κεφ. α. προοίμιον.
div.p: In chronic diseases, delay in treatment is bad; for through negligence they run aground upon incurable affections. By nature they are so constituted that they do not readily depart once they have made an onset. The common reading, φυσίωσις, having no suitable meaning, Ermerins did right in altering this clause, agreeably to the suggestion of Wigan.And if they linger on, in time they become strong and sometimes end only in death; and slight ailments give rise to greater ones in succession, so that even if the earlier condition is free from danger, its offspring becomes fatal. Therefore neither should the patient remain silent out of shame at exposing his disease, nor flee out of fear of the treatment, nor should the physician be remiss; for both conspire toward an incurable outcome. Either ἂν or something else seems to be wanting in this sentence.Some patients, indeed, through ignorance of their present state and of what will follow, live on with their disease to the end; for in most cases they neither perish immediately nor dread death, and on this account they do not even entrust themselves to a physician. Proof of this is afforded by cephalaea, of which I shall speak first.

div.head: Κεφ. β. Θεραπεία Κεφαλαίης.
div.p: Just as the head is indispensable to life, so is it most grievous when diseased; and in affections of the head, the onset is easily borne, consisting of slight pain, ringing in the ears, and heaviness, but if it gathers strength, the final issues are fatal. One must not, therefore, disregard even slight pains, for in some cases they have been cured by slight remedies. If, however, the disease has continued for a long time—since greater burdens supervene—open the vein at the elbow, having given wine to drink for two days beforehand; and gauge the quantity to be drawn by the patient's strength. It is best not to draw it all at once, so that the strength may sustain the amount of depletion and the disease may be dislodged continuously by the same means. This rule, indeed, applies to all chronic diseases. During an interval of three or four days, nourish the patient more liberally; then give the hiera, the purgative medicine, to drink with hydromel, for this especially draws off the nourishment of the disease from the head. The dose of the drug is about four or five drachms by weight. If he is well purged, bathe him, give him wine, and build up his strength; then again open the straight vein on the forehead, for this abstraction is most effective—the quantity being about a cotyla or slightly more. Do not bleed beyond this, for one must not empty the vessels. Next, after shaving off the hair with a razor, apply a cupping instrument first to the crown, and fix another dry one between the shoulder blades; scarify the one on the crown unsparingly, both to draw off a large quantity and to make the incisions deep, for remedies that reach as far as the bone benefit cephalaea. When the wounds have cicatrized, excise the arteries, which are twofold: one pair lies behind the ears slightly further back and is evident by its pulsations; the other lies in front of the ear, close to it, running past the antitragus,

and these too are evident by their pulsations. Cut the larger ones down to the bone, for these are the most beneficial; beside each pair lie others, very slender, which there is no advantage in excising. The method has been described in the surgical treatises. This is a great remedy for cephalaea, epilepsy, vertigo, and in short for all diseases of the head. The common reading, instead of μέγα, is μετά; in Kühn's edition, κατά. The reading I have introduced seems to me self-evident.

Above all, one must draw off phlegm, after first emptying the belly either by a laxative pill or by a clyster: sometimes from the nostrils by errhines, sometimes through the mouth by phlegmagogues. Kinds of errhines are pepper, soapwort root, and castoreum, either singly or combined; having pounded them fine and sifted them, blow them in through a reed or a thick goose-quill. More potent and violent than these is euphorbium mixed with any of them; it is also mixed with oils—gleucinum, Sicyonian oil, or unguent of storax—becoming quite fluid so as to be poured in, and is injected through the nasal 3 tube. These tubes are twin and joined together from a single outlet, so as to inject both nostrils at once; for the distension of each nostril separately is intolerable, as the head immediately swells and sharp pain seizes it. Remedies that draw phlegm through the mouth are mustard, Cnidian berry, pepper, and stavesacre, either together or separately; for chewing them causes continuous spitting. One may also mix them with water or hydromel and give them to rinse the mouth, and pushing the liquid back to the tonsils with the neck extended, gargle with the breath of expiration. When you have drawn off as much phlegm as you wish, bathe the patient and pour very copious warm water over the head to promote transpiration, for strong impactions occur.

Let dinner be frugal, and let there also be wine to restore the stomach, for it too suffers greatly. When in the interval you have established his strength, use the customary clyster, sprinkling in plenty of nitre,
or melting in two drachms by weight of resin from the terebinth tree. On the following day draw blood from inside the nostrils by pushing in the long instrument called cateiadion, or that called toryne; Ermerins does right in substituting this word for στορύνη. See, in particular, Pollux, and the note of Fëos, Oec. Hippocrat., under this word. It was a sort of ladle.or if one lacks these, take the thick quill of a goose feather, scrape it, and notch the fibers into teeth like a saw; pass this into the nostril as far as the ethmoid bones, The common reading in all the editions, except that of Ermerins, is ἰσθμοειδῶν.then twist it with both hands so that the part is scarified by the teeth. The flow of blood is easy and abundant, for slender veins terminate there and the tissues are soft and easily cut. Common people also have many methods of scarification, using rough herbs and dried bay leaves, inserting them with the fingers and rubbing vigorously. When you have evacuated as much as is needed—let the quantity be about half a cotyla—wipe with sponges and oxycrate, or blow in some dry styptic such as oak-gall, split alum, or pomegranate blossom.

If the headache persists after these measures, or even if it ceases for a time, one must carry the treatment through to the end; for it is an evil prone to relapse, and settling in its seat it mostly lurks there. One must therefore shave off the hair with a razor—for this too is beneficial to the head—and cauterize with the knobs of cauteries, Though I have not ventured to change πυρίῃσι into πυρῆνι, I have little doubt that the latter (which signifies the knob of a specillum or cautery) is the true reading. See P. ae. vi. 66, et pluries. superficially down to the muscles; or if you wish to go as far as the bone, keep clear of the muscles, for cauterized muscles provoke convulsions. If you cauterize superficially, pour fragrant white wine with rose oil liberally over the parts, and spread a linen cloth soaked in it over the eschars until the third day; if the eschars are deep,
pound leek leaves with salt, spread them on a linen cloth, and apply them. On the third day apply a cerate of rose oil to the superficial eschars, or lentils with honey to the deep ones. The remedies for cicatrization will be written elsewhere. Some have incised the skin above the forehead along the coronal suture down to the bone, and after scraping or chiseling it down to the diploë, brought it to granulation; others have even trepanned the bone as far as the meninx. These are bold remedies, yet they are to be used if after everything else the cephalaea persists, provided the patient is of good courage and his bodily tone is strong.

If they are gradually recovering, let them take upright exercises for the chest and shoulders, shadow-boxing, throwing of jumping-weights, leaping, and the well-trained rolling that accompanies these; rubbing first and last of the legs, and of the head in the middle.

Apply pitch-plasters continually; Ermerins suppresses τῶ ἐμπάττειν altogether; and seemingly these are superfluous, and unsuitable to this place.and redden the head, sometimes anointing it with mustard mixed with twice as much bread so that the heat may not be intolerable, and sometimes rubbing in compound drugs such as the composition of limnestis, euphorbium, and pyrethrum. For relieving present pain and dislodging the root of the evil, the juice of thapsia is also effective, along with medicines compounded with it that make the skin swell and raise eruptions like pimples.

The diet during each attack of pain should be spare, with little drink and only water, especially before any remedy. In general, abstain from acrid foods—onions, garlic, and silphium juice—though not entirely from mustard, for its sharpness, besides being good for the stomach, is not unwelcome to the head, since it melts phlegm and either disperses it by transpiration or drives it downward. Among legumes the worst is the bean and its varieties—peas, ochrus, and dolichus; next are lentils, which indeed have some virtues for digestion and evacuation, but fill the head and cause pain,
though when boiled with pepper they need not be wholly banished. Washed groats are pleasant with wine and enough honey to sweeten, as are gruel made from them and those cooked in simple broths. Good too in seasoning are the seeds of caraway, coriander, anise, and celery; better than these are the herb mint and pennyroyal, which besides their fragrance have some diuretic power and expel flatulence. Among meats, all aged ones are bad; freshly slaughtered rooster is good, and among birds the wood-pigeon, rock-dove, and others not overly fat; also pigs' feet and roasted hare. Beef and mutton are thickening and fill the head; kid is not altogether bad. Milk and cheeses cause headache. Among fish, rock-fish and whatever are best in the locality. Among boiled vegetables, those that promote urine and loosen the bowels—mallow, blite, beet, asparagus; cabbage too is acrid; among raw ones, lettuce is best of all. Roots are bad even when boiled—radishes, turnips, carrots—for though diuretic they are filling; skirret is flatulent and upsets the stomach. Let wine be white, thin, sweet rather than dry, with just enough astringency not to bind the belly. Every dessert causes headache except dates of all kinds; fresh figs and grapes in season are gentle, as is whatever fruit is best in its season. The common reading is σύκων δὲ ὀπώρη, which Ermerins has altered to ὀπώρης δὲ σῦκα. It will be seen that, by a less violent change, I have succeeded in amending the text.Repletion from anything, even from beneficial things, is bad, and indigestion is worse; fatigue is less harmful than indigestion, yet harmful too. Walks in the morning after evacuating the bowels, where the air is fresh and pleasant; walks after dinner are also excellent. Long passive rides, sheltered from wind and sun for the head, for the Dog Star is bad for it. Sexual intercourse is a self-inflicted evil for the head and nerves. Travel from cold regions to warmer ones, and from damp to drier; a sea voyage and living at sea are beneficial; and if one lives by the coast, it is good to bathe in cold brine,
to swim in the sea, to roll in the sands, and to live by the sea.

The remedies for heterocrania are the same; for whatever remedies are suited to the whole head are equally good to use for any part of the head. For those in whom the disease does not yield to these measures, one must use hellebore, the ultimate and most powerful of all treatments.

div.head: Κεφ. γ. Θεραπεία Σκοτωματικῶν.
div.p: Vertigo arises both in succession to cephalaea and also independently from its own causes—suppression of hemorrhoidal flow, or when blood ceases to flow from the nose where it formerly flowed, or when the body no longer transpires through sweat or exertion where it formerly labored. If, then, it has arisen from cephalaea, one must apply for its cure all the measures stated under cephalaea; what more violent remedies must be used at the end of treatment I shall tell later. If the disease has resulted from some suppression of fluids, stimulate the accustomed evacuation, for the return of nature to its course is healthful. If, however, this delays while the affection increases, in the case of other suppressions—through the nose or sweats—open the vein at the elbow; if it arises from an engorged liver or spleen or any of the middle viscera, cupping is helpful. One must draw from these parts as much blood as would flow freely from a vein, for this is the nourishment of the cause, as is also the stomach. To this join the remedies for the head: opening the straight vein on the forehead, or those on either side of the nose near the corners of the eyes; applying a cupping instrument to the crown; excising the arteries; shaving the head; reddening it; drawing off phlegm through the nostrils by errhines or through the mouth, as I have described; doing everything in the order stated under cephalaea, except with the addition of cyclamen juice or pimpernel juice poured into the nose.

When you have come to the end of the remedies for the head, the more violent measures to be used for vertiginous patients are these: one must employ emetics after dinner and those from radishes, which are also needed as preparation for hellebore; for the stomach must be trained to vomit before the more severe emetics, and the phlegm now becomes thinner and more easily discharged by hellebore. There are several ways of administering hellebore: to the stronger patients give it cut to the size of a sesame seed Ermerins, following the suggestion of Petit, substitutes this word for ἄμης, which is quite unsuitable to the place.or slightly coarser, administered with washed groats or lentils, the weight being two drachms; to the weaker and leaner give the decoction with honey, the measure being two or three spoonfuls; the method of preparing this will be described elsewhere. Between each remedy, nourish the patient to enable him to endure the intermediate treatments.

Give aid during the paroxysms as follows: bind the legs above the ankles and knees, and the wrists and upper arms below the shoulders near the elbows. Foment the head with rose oil and vinegar, having boiled wild thyme, sphondylium, ivy, or the like in the oil. Rub the extremities and face; apply to the nostrils vinegar, pennyroyal, and mint, also with vinegar. Pry open the jaw, for sometimes they clench their jaws tightly; tickle the tonsils to provoke vomiting, for sometimes upon a discharge of phlegm they have awakened from the darkness. These measures, then, serve to relieve the paroxysm and dispel the gloom.

Concerning the entire regimen during treatment and afterward, my judgment is as follows. Much sleep is bad, and so is sleeplessness. Much sleep benumbs the senses of the head; by the flooding of vapors there is sluggishness toward every action. Ermerins suppresses this clause altogether.These things, moreover, are causes of heaviness,
ringing in the ears, and flashes before the eyes—the signs of the disease. Sleeplessness, on the other hand, impairs digestion and nutrition, exhausts the body, causes despondency, and makes the mind easily led astray, so that such patients readily fall into mania and melancholy. Moderate sleep is beneficial for the assimilation of food and for rest from the day's labors. Forethought and persistence Ermerins also erases these words, which do not seem to be needed. See, further, Petit and Wigan.must give first place to the evacuation of the bowels, for the belly is the principal cause of transpiration. Next, rub the legs with rough linen towels until they redden, then the back and sides, and last the head. After this, take walks—gentle at the beginning and toward the end, brisk in the middle; let there be rest and settling of the breath after walking. One should practice vocal exercises, using rather the deep tones; for high-pitched tones cause distension of the head, throbbing of the temples, pulsation of the brain, swelling of the eyes, and ringing in the ears, whereas moderate high-pitched voice is very beneficial to the head. Next comes the time for passive exercise, to disperse all heaviness of the head; let it be long, yet without causing fatigue, and let it not be taken along winding places or continual turns, for these provoke vertigo. Let walks also be straight, long, and level. If the patients are accustomed to breakfast, give bread alone, only so much as will not impede their exercises, for it must be digested beforehand. Rub the head and hands gently to recall warmth, good flesh, and tone; then let the head be rubbed while standing upright, held up to someone taller than oneself. Exercises should also be directed properly toward strengthening the neck and extending the arms; keeping the head raised, let him train his eyes by shadow-boxing, throwing the discus, or sparring in boxing. Ball-playing, whether with a small or large ball, is bad, for the whirling and straining of the head and eyes produce vertigo.

Leaping and running are excellent, for all brisk movement of the legs tones the whole body. Cold bathing is better than no bathing, and no bathing is better than hot bathing: cold bathing is most potent to brace, condense, and dry the head—the condition of health—whereas hot bathing is most potent to moisten, relax, and cloud it, which are the causes of disease of the head; and such too are south winds, which dull the hearing. Rest after exercises to calm the agitation; press the head to scrape the skin.

For morning drinks, water or diluted wine; a frugal breakfast of softening potherbs—mallow, beet, blite—with a sauce that is wholesome for the stomach, palatable, laxative, and light on the head, made with thyme, savory, or mustard. Eggs warm in winter and cold in summer, soft-boiled out of the shell, not roasted; olives, dates, pickled fish in season, and washed groats with some sweetening to taste are desirable, along with salt. Then quiet and rest for both hearing and speech; walks where the air is fresh and pleasant, among trees or herbs. When dinner approaches, it is best to take a cold bath again after anointing slightly with oil; if not, wash the legs only. Let dinner be farinaceous, such as pastry, gruel of groats, or non-flatulent barley-gruel well boiled for easy digestion; the seasonings to make the barley-gruel palatable are pepper, pennyroyal, mint, and a little onion or leek, not enough to float on the stomach; sharp vinegar is beneficial. Among meats, the lean parts of fat animals, pigs' feet and head, and all birds—judging by quantity—as well as hare and game; fowl is readily available and beneficial. Every dessert causes headache except dates, ripe figs, or grapes, provided the patient is not flatulent; and of cakes, those that are digestible, not greasy, and light. Then walks, cheerfulness, and retiring to sleep in quiet.

div.head: Κεφ. δ. Θεραπεία Ἐπιληψίης.
div.p: One must employ whatever remedies are great and most powerful against epilepsy; for it is an escape not only from a painful and dangerous affection at every recurrence, but also from ugliness of appearance and the reproach of the calamity. Indeed, it seems to me that if the sufferers looked at one another during their paroxysms and saw all that they endure, they would no longer bear to live; yet insensibility and blindness hide from each his own terrors and disgrace. It is best for medical treatment to accompany the relief afforded by nature when, through the changes of age, she greatly alters the person; for if the habitual regimen of the evil, in which the disease lives, departs, it no longer visits the person, but departs together with its former delight.

If, then, it has seized upon the head and dwells there, one must do everything that I have stated regarding cephalaea, both in respect of bloodletting—and of purgings I wonder that Ermerins should have thought it necessary to expunge these words. It appears to me that, from the commencement of this paragraph down to τλήμονας, we have one of those long and complicated sentences in which Thucydides, Demosthenes, and other of the great writers of antiquity delighted. This style of composition is very different from the periodic style in which Roman, French, and English authors compose their works. Clarendon, Milton, and Cobbett are the best examples we have, in English, of the old Grecian style of writing in long sentences.—opening the veins at the elbow, the straight vein of the forehead, and cupping; yet bloodletting must not be carried to the point of fainting, for fainting provokes the affection. Cut all the arteries, both before and behind the ears; and perform purgings as outlets for all these humors, using the hiera purgative and remedies that draw phlegm from the head, though the drugs should be much stronger, for the constitution of these patients endures the hardship, while cheerfulness and good hope make them steadfast. One must also apply fire to the head, for it is effective: first perforate the bone
down to the diploë, then use cerates and poultices until the meninx separates from the bones; cut away the bare portions with a trepan if they still slightly adhere, until they detach spontaneously—when the meninx is sometimes found black and thick—and when, after suppuration or cleansing under the physician's bold treatment, the wound cicatrizes, the patient is delivered from the disease. Above all, use rubefacients on the head—the usual ones I have mentioned earlier, and more powerfully that made with cantharides; before using this, however, the patient must drink milk for three days to protect the bladder, for cantharides severely injure the bladder. These measures, then, if the head is affected.

If, however, the middle parts introduce the cause and bring on the disease—though this happens very rarely, since the middle parts rather sympathize with the head as in a great evil than serve as the origin of the disease—however that may be, open the vein at the elbow in these cases too, for the flow comes from the viscera; and purge these patients more than others with the hiera, cneorum, and Cnidian berry, for these draw off phlegm. The most timely remedy for them is cupping. The multitude of plasters and poultices is well known, and it is superfluous to describe them all, except to know their power: that with them one must attenuate, promote transpiration, and render the parts free-flowing and well-ventilated, using digestive, heating, drying, and diuretic drugs both in food and in medicine. Best of all is castoreum drunk in hydromel several times a month, and whatever compound medicines do the same—the compound theriac of vipers, and the even more complex antidote of Mithridates; let him also drink that of Vestinus, for these are digestive, wholesome, and diuretic. As for all the simple drugs one might list, these compounds contain their powers: cinnamon, cassia, malabathrum leaves, and all kinds of pepper and hartwort—what indeed of the most potent remedies would you not find in them? Report says that the brain of a vulture,
the raw heart of a cormorant, and domestic weasels That this is the true reading, and not οἱ ἐνοικάδιοι γαλεοὶ, is quite obvious from Dioscorides, ii. 27. All the γαλεοὶ were sea animals. See Appendix to Dunbar's Greek Lexicon.when eaten dissolve the disease. I have never tried these myself; I have, however, seen people hold a cup beneath the wound of a freshly slain man and drink a draught of the blood. O the dire necessity present, to dare to cure an evil with an evil pollution! Whether any were actually restored to health by this, no one can tell me with certainty. Another account prescribed eating human liver. Let these things be recorded for those who can bring themselves to go so far.

One must also assist with regimen and with every circumstance, whether managed by others or by the patient himself. Here nothing must be overlooked and nothing done at random, aiming in every small detail at what is wholly beneficial, or if not, at least harmless. Ermerins, following the advice of Petit, by the addition of μὴ, and slightly altering the punctuation, greatly improves the text in this place. Our author evidently alludes to the celebrated passage in the Epidemics of Hippocrates. See vol. i. p. 360, Syd. Soc. Edit.For countless sights that ought not to be viewed, sounds, tastes, and odors bring the disease to light. Be exceedingly careful, therefore, about everything. Much sleep produces thickness, sluggishness, and a mist over the senses; moderation is good. Evacuation of the bowels after sleep is excellent, especially of wind and phlegm. Long, straight, uncurved walks in fresh air under myrtle or bay trees, or among sharp and fragrant herbs—calamint, pennyroyal, thyme, mint—preferably wild and self-grown, or if not, even cultivated ones; among these also long, straight passive rides. It is good to make journeys, yet not beside a river gazing at the current (for a flowing stream produces dizziness), nor looking at a turning wheel or a spinning top, The common reading is μηδὲ ἐν κύκλῳ στροφούμενον, for which Ermerins proposes to substitute the above, on the authority of a Parisian ms.for the patient is too weak
to keep his spirit steady, and it whirls round with the circle; and whirling provokes vertigo and epilepsy. After passive exercise, a quiet walk, then rest to calm the agitation of the ride. After this, exercises with the hands, the extremities having been rubbed with unbleached linen towels; I have not scrupled, in this sentence, to follow Ermerins in substituting τριβέντων for ἐνόντων, which has no meaning suitable to the place. The passage is still obscure.anointing not overly oily; friction slow Instead of ἐν μελλήσει, Ermerins reads ἐμμέλης. I am doubtful.and rather firm to condense the flesh, for most patients are swollen and thick. In the middle of the whole rubbing, let the head be rubbed upright. Exercises for the neck and shoulders, shadow-boxing, and everything I have described for vertiginous patients—no need to repeat all that here, except that their exercises should be brisker to induce sweat and warmth, since all this attenuates the humors. Throughout their whole life, moreover, one should cultivate a quick spirit free from anger.

All foods made of thick legumes are bad; among cereal foods, rather dry bread, washed groats, and gruels made from them; the seasonings are the same as before, though now with more acrid ones—pepper, ginger, lovage. Sauces made with vinegar and cumin are both pleasant and useful. From meats let him abstain altogether if possible, or at least during treatment; during recovery, let them be those light by nature, such as birds except duck, and light in digestion, such as hares, pigs' feet, and pickled fish; and with these, thirst is good. Little wine, white, thin, fragrant, and diuretic. Among boiled vegetables, those acrid in power to attenuate and promote urine, such as cabbage, asparagus, and nettle; among raw ones, lettuce in season. Cucumber and melon are superfluous for a strong man, though to some a taste may be granted, for a large quantity of them is bad since they are cold and moist. Fresh figs and grapes
are seasonable. Walks, and after them untroubled cheerfulness.

Anger and lust are bad, for the very act bears the signs of the disease. There is a mistaken notion regarding intercourse even among some physicians: because nature's transition to manhood accomplishes some good, they have forced the nature of boys by premature intercourse as if to restore them sooner, ignorant of nature's spontaneous appointed term at which all cures occur. For nature brings forth what belongs to each age in due season: in due time come the ripening of seed, of the beard, and of gray hair. What physician, then, could alter nature's original change of seed or her appointed term for each stage? On the contrary, they have actually aggravated the nature of the disease, for some are no longer fit when the proper time for intercourse arrives, having been injured beforehand by its unseasonable practice.
One should live in warm, dry regions, for the disease is cold and moist.

div.head: Κεφ. ε. Θεραπεία Μελαγχολίης.
div.p:
Careful judgment is required concerning bloodletting in melancholics, from which humor the disease arises—as well as from bad humors—and not merely when there is a small quantity. If, then, it seizes a young person and in the spring season, open the median vein at the right elbow, so that the flow may come opportunely from the liver; for that viscus is the fountain of blood and the source of bile, both of which are the nourishment of melancholy. Open the vein even if they are lean and deficient in blood, but draw off only a little—just enough for the strength to feel the incision without being compromised in its tone. For even if the blood is thick, bilious, congealed, and black like olive-lees, yet this is the seat and nourishment of nature; if, therefore, you draw off more than is proper, nature is driven from its
seat by lack of nourishment. If the patient is plethoric, the blood is usually not very bad: open the vein, and do not draw all that is needed on the same day, but at intervals—or on the same day, as the patient's strength will indicate. In the interval, nourish more liberally so that he may endure another evacuation. One must also aid the stomach, both because it is diseased and because black bile settles in it. After a spare diet for one day beforehand, give black hellebore with hydromel, about two drachms by weight, for this purges black bile; the tops of Attic thyme also carry off black bile, and it is best to mix one part of each to make two drachms of both together. Bathe him after the purging, give a little wine, and the other comforts of food, for purging is exhausting to the strength of the stomach. Next turn again to the middle parts: after first relaxing them with a poultice and fomentation, apply a cupping instrument over the liver and the belly, or its orifice, for this abstraction is far more timely than venesection; apply it also to the back between the shoulder blades, where the stomach is attached. Then nourish him again, and when his strength has revived through diet, shave the head and apply a cupping instrument to the head; for the primary and greatest cause of the disease lies in the nerves. Wigan and Ermerins have very properly substituted this word for νούσοισι. Petit suggests ἐν τοῖσι ἄλλοισι.Nor are the senses unharmed, since their origin and beginning is from there; they too are altered, sharing in the affection, and some patients even suffer hallucinations from derangement of the senses. Above all one must aid the stomach, both as being itself diseased and as the seat where black bile lodges. Give, therefore, juice of wormwood to drink continually, from a small amount up to a cyathus, for this prevents the generation of bile; aloes too is good, for it carries bile down into the lower
intestine. If, then, the affection is recent and the patient is not greatly deranged, no further medical treatment is needed beyond this, only the remaining regimen to restore his constitution, thoroughly cleanse the affection, and strengthen his powers so that the disease may not relapse; I shall describe the regimen of convalescence later.

If, however, after shrinking back slightly under these measures, the disease appears again, greater remedies are needed. Let there be no delay: if the disease is present owing to retention of the menses in a woman or of hemorrhoidal flow in a man, stimulate the parts to discharge some of the accustomed flow. If it delays and does not come, the blood having been diverted elsewhere while the disease presses on, make evacuations for him, beginning from the ankles; and if you cannot draw enough from there, open the vein at the elbow as well. After three or four days of nourishing, give the hiera purgative to drink; then apply a cupping instrument to the middle parts, close to the liver, and carry out the measures with all speed. For melancholy does not yield to slight remedies, and if one delays the great ones, it settles firmly in its seat; and once it inhabits the whole body—senses, mind, blood, bile—and lays hold of the nerves as well, it both turns incurable itself and engenders The common reading, ἐγκοτεῖ, being evidently inadmissible, I have preferred the reading adopted by Ermerins, in preference to ἐγκροτεῖ, as suggested by Petit, or ἐγκύει as proposed by Wigan.in the body the offspring of other diseases—convulsion, mania, paralysis; and when these arise from melancholy, the resulting conditions are incurable. Use hellebore, therefore, to cure the evil. Before hellebore, however, one must train the stomach to vomit, attenuate the humors, and render the body free-flowing; emetics accomplish this, sometimes fasting and sometimes with radishes. I shall describe both the method and the materials, as well as the kinds of hellebore, the modes of using it,
how to prepare each patient beforehand, and how to assist during the vomiting. It is incredible if the disease is not completely dissolved by these measures, or at least does not have remissions of many years, for melancholies are generally the offspring of this humor. Yet if it remains steadfast, wait no longer, but carry out all the measures for hellebore. To restore all sick people to health is indeed impossible, for then a physician would be greater than a god; Hippocrat. Prognost.but to procure freedom from pain, remissions, and latency of diseases is lawful for a physician to accomplish. Either, then, one must give up and decline such cases, pleading their incurability, or else carry the work through to the end. Give also the hiera made with aloes from time to time, for this is a timely remedy for melancholy, serving to purge the stomach, liver, and bile. Likewise, to drink about a drachm by weight of mallow seed with water has been proven by experience to be excellent; and countless other simple drugs are useful in different cases.

After these hardships, lead the patient into convalescence. For in some cases the disease was dislodged from its seat during the period of treatment, and when the person comes to the restoration of flesh and strength, all traces of the disease are driven away together; for strength of nature produces health, while weakness produces disease. Let the patient, therefore, depart for convalescence to live at natural hot springs; for the medicinal substances in them are beneficial It is so accented in all the mss. and editions.—bitumen, sulfur, alum, and many other virtues besides. Moisture is good after the dryness of the disease and the hardship of the treatment; loose and soft flesh is easiest for throwing off the disease, whereas the flesh of melancholics is dry and dense. Oily inunction with gentle rubbing, receiving plenty of oil washed bread with some sweet wine, Cretan siraeum Wigan has substituted this reading for θηραίῳ τῷ κρητί.and Pamphylian scybelites,
or wine and honey of an old mixture; eggs both cool and warm, soft-boiled out of the shell; meats not fat and detergent—pigs' feet and head, lean wings of birds, and among wild animals hare, gazelle, and leveret; of autumn fruits, whatever is best. In the case of regurgitation from the stomach, take care before meals that what is swallowed is not vomited up: give, therefore, half a cyathus of hydromel before all food, and after drinking it let him vomit to cleanse the stomach, for thus your food will stay firmly down. Necessary cleansing remedies are pine-nuts, nettle seed, coccalus seeds, pepper, and bitter almonds, bound together with honey. If you wish to dry the humors, myrrh, iris root, the theriac of vipers, that of Vestinus, that of Mithridates, and countless others are excellent. For external applications, the materials for poultices are melilot, poppies, terebinth resin, hyssop, and oil of roses or of wild vine-blossom, with wax as the base for all of them. Oily inunction, passive rides, walks, and everything else that rebuilds flesh, strengthens the powers, and restores nature to its former state.

div.head: Κεφ. η. Θεραπεία Φθίσιος.
div.p:
as in a ship in calm weather; for if the patient is fortunate, his passive exercise and manner of life should be at sea, since sea-air imparts a certain dryness to the ulcers. After passive exercise and rest, let him be anointed with rich oil, continually poured on during the rubbings gradually from a small quantity up to five or six cotylae, or much more; or if not, as much as he can take, for often this alone has sufficed instead of all other food. Milk is pleasant to take, easiest to drink,
solid in nourishing, and more familiar from childhood than any other food; it is pleasing to the eye in color, a medicine for the windpipe that smooths roughness, clears the bronchus, brings up phlegm, eases breathing, and lubricates the downward passage; and for ulcers it is a sweet medicine, gentler than any other. If, then, one drinks much of it, there is no need of any other food—for it is a good thing in disease when milk serves at once as medicine and as food; indeed, the milk-drinking nations of mankind do not eat grain. Excellent with milk are porridges, pastries, washed groats, and all dishes made from milk. If other food is needed, let it be similar: barley-gruel, easily digested and plain, seasoned only so much as to make it easiest to sip; and if anything is added for flavor, let that too be medicinal—lovage leaves, pennyroyal, mint, a little salt, vinegar, or honey. If the stomach digests poorly, give this; if nothing compels otherwise, barley-gruel is better than anything. One may also exchange barley-gruel for groats, for it is less flatulent, more digestible, and detergent if pounded like barley-gruel. The common reading is ἢν καὶ ὡς πτισάνη μιγματώδης ὀπτίσθω; which Ermerins alters to σμηγματώδης πτισθῆ, the meaning of which seems to me very equivocal.In moister expectorations, beans cleanse ulcers, though they are flatulent; peas and ochrus, by as much as they are less flatulent, are less cleansing for ulcers. Judging, therefore, according to present circumstances, make use of these, with the same seasonings as stated for barley-gruel. Eggs from the fire, watery and warm; best of all are those freshly laid by the birds, before the

div.head: Κεφ. ιγ. Θεραπεία Ἥπατος.
div.p:
an ulcer in the liver is fatal. The most grievous confluence of pus is into the stomach, if it takes the esophagus as its path for upward discharge; for food is the cause of life, and the leader of food
is the esophagus, which also conveys medicines to the inner parts. If, therefore, a loathing of swallowing everything sets in, the patient must swiftly die of both disease and starvation. The signs of each place toward which the pus will turn are different: if it passes through the intestines, there are griping pains, loose bowels, phlegm and bile, then along with the flux clots of blood or washings like raw meat; if into the bladder, heaviness in the kidneys and loins—at first the urine is copious and bile-stained, then turbid, without sediment and unsettled, and finally a white sediment appears; if it tends upward to the stomach, there is nausea, loss of appetite, vomiting of phlegm or bile, fainting, and vertigo until it bursts.

Above all, then, one must divert this upward course, for the path is bad. If the pus flows rather violently, one must do everything to assist the stomach with foods, medicines, and regimen, all gently. For medicines to promote the rupture of the abscess, give the herb hyssop to drink with hydromel, and leaves of horehound also with hydromel and juice of wormwood; these must be drunk before meals so that the humors may become thin, the passages free-flowing, and the suppurating parts easy to rupture. Give also asses' milk, which is smooth, free from bile, nourishing, and does not curdle into cheese—which is the virtue of milk. Add also pleasant flavors to drink and food; even if they are slightly inferior to the most beneficial things, give them, since there will be a passage for a nauseating and unpleasant fluid, and the transit of pus harms some patients, so that they become averse to food and readily vomit whatever they take. Even in the other outlets one must take every care of the stomach, for it is the pathway for all medicines; and one must also remember the liver, where the root of the ulcers lies. Though I have not ventured to alter the text, I must say that I think the true reading would be φλεβῶν, instead of ἑλκέων. I cannot see the significance of the latter, whereas the former is of frequent use with our author as applied to the liver.If it tends toward the bladder, draw it off with diuretics:
the roots of asarum, valerian, maidenhair, and spignel as drinks, taken with hydromel. Among compounds, the medicine of Vestinus and that made with winter-cherries are excellent, as well as whatever is commended by experience. If you direct it through the intestines, you have milk as a laxative—best is asses' milk, or failing that, goats' or sheep's milk; also slippery and detergent gruels, such as barley-gruel, with pepper, ginger, and lovage as seasonings. To speak generally of the entire diet upon every rupture: foods should be wholesome, good for the stomach, and easily digested—either gruels, or porridges made with milk, starch, and pastries with milk.

div.head: Κεφ. ιδ. Θεραπεία Σπληνός.
div.p: Dissolving a scirrhus Liddel and Scott, conformably to analogy, but in opposition to general usage, read σκῖρος.of the spleen is not very easy; and if secondary diseases arise from it—dropsy or cachexia—the evil runs aground upon an incurable state for the physician to cure the scirrhus. One must therefore prevent them from forming and dissolve them when just beginning, opposing the inflammations of which scirrhi are the sequel are brought to transpiration the abscess; for these belong to inflammation. Use the remedies I have described under acute diseases. If despite all your efforts during inflammation the scirrhus persists, use remedies resembling fire to soften the hardness: fomentations of vinegar, oil, and honey, with folded linen cloths instead of wool; sprinkle on sifted ben-nut, and apply the most emollient poultices.

div.head: ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ *β.

head.foreign: Κεφαλὴ πρώτη λείπει. Κεφ. β. Θεραπεία Διαβήτο υ.

div.p: The affection of diabetes is a species of dropsy in both cause and condition, differing only in the place through which the fluid flows out. For in ascites the receptacle is the peritoneum, and it has no outlet, but remaining there it accumulates; whereas in diabetes the rush of fluid from the sufferer and the melting of the flesh are the same, while the discharge conveys it to the kidneys and bladder for exit. This same pathway occurs in dropsical patients when the disease turns for the better—though what is truly good is the dissolution of the cause, not merely relief from the burden. In diabetics, however, thirst is greater, for the outflowing fluid dries them up.

The remedies for checking the melting are the same as for dropsy, but for the thirst great medical care is required, since in this form it is the greatest of all sufferings; and if they drink any fluid, it provokes urination, and as it rushes out it carries away with it the melting tissues of the body. There is need, therefore, of thirst-quenching medicines; for the thirst is great through insatiability of drink, since no amount of drink becomes a cure for the thirst. By every means one must aid the stomach, where
the springs of thirst lie. When, therefore, you have purged with the hiera, use external applications of nard, mastic, dates, and raw quinces: their juice with nard and rose oil is excellent for fomentation, and their pulp with mastic and dates as a poultice; mixing them in wax and nard ointment is good, or the juices of acacia and hypocist both for fomentations and for poultices.

Let the drinking water also be boiled with autumn fruits. For food, milk and with it cereals—starch, groats, gruels. Astringent wines to tone the stomach, rather undiluted, to disperse and wash away the other humors, for thirst comes from salty humors; and wine that is at once astringent and cooling is useful for altering and tempering them. This word, or some other of similar import, is evidently required in this place, as Petit was the first to suggest. Ermerins does not hesitate to adopt it.For strength, sweet wine also, resembling blood, to generate blood. The compound medicines are the same: that of vipers, that of Mithridates, that of autumn fruits, and whatever else is beneficial for dropsy; and the entire diet and manner of life are the same.

div.head: Κεφ. γ. Θεραπεία λιθιάσε ως καὶ ἑλκώσεως Νεφρῶν.
div.p: Concerning inflammation, hemorrhage, and whatever kills acutely from the kidneys, I have written under acute diseases; concerning ulceration and the formation of stones, which generally accompany old men until death, I write now—as close to a cure as possible, or if not, the means by which the patient may be relieved.

To turn a constitution naturally disposed to form stones into a barren one is impossible; for it is easier to make a womb barren than to make stone-forming kidneys
free of stones. How to aid their passage, however, and what remedies to use when stones become lodged in place, I shall explain. For they cause severe pain, and sometimes patients have died from griping pains, ileus of the colon, and retention of urine, since the kidneys and colon are closely connected. If, then, there is impaction of stones accompanied by retention of urine and griping pains, open the vein at the ankle on the side corresponding to the kidney; for discharges of blood from the kidneys relax the constriction around the stones, since inflammation binds and holds everything fast, and depletion of the vessels dissolves inflammation. Foment the loins where the kidneys lie; let old or new oil contain rue, and diuretic too are dill leaves, rosemary, or marjoram—with these one should pour liberally as with water, for mere anointings do little. Apply vapor-baths with these as well, pouring chamomile oil into ox-bladders; the materials for poultices are the same, combined with meals. Dry cupping has sometimes loosened the impaction of stones, and it is excellent also to scarify when there is inflammation. If despite these measures the stones still remain, place the patient in a bath of oil; for this does everything at once—it relaxes by warmth, lubricates, and its pungency stimulates the urge to expel—and these are the means of exit and expulsion for stones. For simple medicines to drink: roots of valerian, spignel, and asarum; herbs such as betony, parsley, or water-parsnip; and among compounds, ointments containing nard, cassia, myrrh, and cinnamon. In the Askew ms. there is a lacuna here, occupying a whole page, but none at the end of the chapter, as in the printed editions.
For cicatrization, mustard, eschars from fire, and the applications I have mentioned before; and diet, inunction, sea voyages, and living by the sea are all remedies for kidney affections.

div.head: Κεφ. ε. Θεραπεία Γονορροίης.
div.p: Both on account of the unpleasantness of the affection, the danger of wasting, and the need for the continuation of the race, one must lose no time in curing gonorrhea, which is the cause of all evils. First of all, then, treat it like an ordinary flux: by astringents applied to the parts around the bladder and the seat of the flow, and by cooling the loins, flanks, genitals, and testicles so that the semen may not flow out copiously; then afterward warm the whole region in order to dry up the passages. For astringents and fomentations: unwashed wool from the sheep with its grease, and oil of roses or of wild vine-blossom with fragrant white wine. Gradually warming, use fresh oil with melilot boiled in it, marjoram, rosemary, or fleabane; dill leaves are excellent, and still better is rue. Use these in poultices with barley-meal, vetch-meal, hedge-mustard seed, and nitre, with honey to bind and unite them all. Suitable too are poultices that redden the skin, raise pimples, divert the flux, and warm the parts—such as the green plaster and that made with bay berries. Give also castoreum frequently to drink, about a drachm by weight of winter-cherry root, and a decoction of mint; among compounds, the medicine of the two peppers, Symphonus's, and Philo's; excellent too is the potion made with the skink lizard, that of Vestinus, and that made with vipers. Entrust the whole mainly to regimen, relying upon exercises, walks, and passive rides, for these turn the constitution toward warmth, which is what the affection needs; and if the patient is also temperate in sexual matters and bathes in cold water, there is hope that he will recover his manhood very quickly.

div.head: Κεφ. ς. Θεραπεία Στομαχικῶν .
div.p: In other affections, the regimen after treatment is good for restoring bodily strength and vigor through easy digestion; in stomachic patients alone, however, this fails. How it should be managed, then, I shall explain. Passive rides, walks, exercise, vocal exercise, and digestible foods are capable of combating loathing of food in the stomach, yet these cannot dissolve prolonged indigestion or turn the emaciation of the body into plump flesh. Far greater in these patients must be the indulgences shown to the sick, doing everything with cleanliness, and the physician's compliance with their cravings when they do no great harm; for this is best, unless a craving arises for things that are not at all beneficial. For medicinal drinks: juices, wormwood, nard ointment, Ermerins erases τὸ μύρον, fancying that the ointment could not be suitable in this place. However, Actuarius recommends the Nardinum Unguentum expressly for Stomachics. Meth. Med. vi. 10.the theriac of vipers, and the seed of rock-parsley, If the text here be sound, the expression must be understood as a strange circumlocution for πετροσελίνου or σελίνου τοῦ ἐν πέτραις. See below, in the next chapter. It is worthy of remark, that this mode of circumlocution was much practised by the writers in the Ionic dialect. See Gregorius Corinthus, under περὶ Ἰάδος.ginger, pepper, and hartwort—these are digestives. Over the chest, as an astringent application, use nard, mastic, aloes, acacia, quince juice, and the very pulp of quinces crushed with dates as an astringent plaster; and also all the other remedies I have written for diabetes to cure thirst, for the same thirst occurs in these patients too, and tone of the stomach frees stomachic patients from thirst.

div.head: Κεφ. ζ. Θεραπεία Κοιλιακῶν.
div.p: When the belly is unable to retain food and nourishment passes straight through undigested, unassimilated, and raw, adding nothing to the body's bulk, we call such patients celiacs—owing to chilling of the innate heat for digestion and weakness of the faculty of distribution.

First of all, therefore, one must relieve the belly from labor by rest and fasting, for thus its powers return. If there is also a sensation of fullness in the stomach, use fasting emetics with water or hydromel. Cover and foment the belly for astringency with unwashed sheep's wool and oil of roses, wild vine-blossom, or quinces—or best of all mastic oil—with hypocist or omphacium; along with these, poultices warm to the touch yet astringent in power. If there is tension or inflammation anywhere about the liver or the orifice of the stomach, apply a cupping instrument and scarify, which alone has sufficed for some; and when the wounds have cicatrized under cerates and hardness remains, apply leeches to the spot. Then apply digestive plasters such as that of seeds, provided it contains chameleon root; excellent too are those with bay berries, the emollient called the green plaster, and my own "mystery" plaster, for these soften, irritate, rouse warmth, and free the viscera from flatulence, which is needed for astringency. Mustard, limnestis, euphorbium, and all such remedies likewise prevent chilling and recall warmth. Similar medicines should also be given to drink for astringency: first needed plantain juice with water made astringent with myrtle berries or quinces; excellent too are grape-seeds from unripe grapes, and the most astringent wines. Next, medicinal drinks that heal the
belly—those made with ginger, pepper, and the seed of wild rock-parsley; the theriac of vipers is most digestive. If under these measures the disease yields nothing or very little, use radish emetics; and if you insert white hellebore root into the radishes for a single night, your purge will be most vigorous, both for cleansing and evacuating cold humors and for kindling heat.

Let the diet and manner of life also be suited to these patients: sleep by night, and by day walks, vocal exercises, passive rides among bay trees, myrtles, or thyme—for the exhalation and inhalation of such plants have a digestive medicinal virtue; exercises, rubbings, shadow-boxing, exercises of the chest and belly by throwing jumping-weights; morning drinks, for a tiny portion of bread is light and bracing; after these, rubefaction, leisurely walks

div.head: Κεφ. ιβ. Θεραπεία Ἀρθρίτιδος καὶ Ἰσχιάδος.
div.p:
food and radishes frequently; There can be little or no doubt that the words in the lacuna immediately adjoining σιτίων, were ἔμετος ἀπό. On the popular modes of producing easy vomiting in ancient times, see Pαυλυς aeγινετα, t. i, pp. 52 — 54. On the use of emetics in the cure of Arthritis and Schiatica, see further, Ibid t. i. pp. 652 — 676, πασσιμ.then lead on to hellebore. The diet afterward is common to the other affections; and with the diet, inunction and cold sea-bathing. For the most part, indeed, the remedies are common to all arthritic patients; for even in gouty patients hellebore is the great remedy, though in the first attacks of the affection—if it has already lasted for a long
time and has also appeared by inheritance from parents, the disease stays until death. For paroxysms of the joints, do as follows: use unwashed sheep's wool with its grease, and fomentations of rose oil and wine; in some cases a sponge with oxycrate has helped. Then a poultice of bread with cooling things—gourd, melon, plain cucumber, the herb plantain, and rose petals; ironwort too relieves pain with bread, as do moss, comfrey root, the herb cinquefoil, and fine-leaved horehound (a decoction of this last is a soothing lotion, and the herb itself is a poultice with bread-crumbs or barley-meal). The inedible part of citrons with barley-meal is excellent, as are dried figs and Thasian almonds with some meal. These, then, are the cooling materials; and one thing helps one person at one time and the same helps another at another time. There is evidently something wanting in the text. Petit and Ermerins substitute ὠφελέει after ἄλλῳ. I cannot but think, however, that the more natural reading would be μὴ; meaning, that the remedies in certain cases proved beneficial, and in others not.To some patients, warming remedies are beneficial, and the same thing helps different people at different times. Report also says that the following is very soothing: let a goat graze on the herb iris, and when it is full, after waiting until the fodder is worked up in its belly, slaughter the goat and bury the patient's feet in the dung inside its belly. Medicines are countless, for misfortune makes the sufferers themselves resourceful pharmacists; the medicines of physicians will be set forth in the pharmacological treatises.

div.head: Κεφ. ιγ. Θεραπεία Ἐλέφαντος.
div.p:
The remedies for diseases must be greater than the diseases to dissolve them; yet for so great an evil as elephantiasis, what treatment could be a match? For the evil does not strike only a single part or viscus, nor merely creep within or
without, but dwells inwardly throughout the entire person and encompasses him wholly from without. It is loathsome and dreadful to behold—for it has the aspect of a wild beast—and people fear to live and associate with the sufferer no less than with the plague, since infection is easily communicated through breathing. What remedy, then, worthy of this disease could one find in medicine? The common reading, ἄξιον ἔχον, is changed by Ermerins to ἀξιόνικον. I cannot see that this change is any improvement.Yet one must bring together every resource—drugs, regimen, iron, and fire; and if you apply these while the affection is still newly born, there is hope of cure, but if it has reached full growth, sits firmly in the viscera, and also attacks the face, the patient is beyond hope.

Open, therefore, the veins at the elbow—both of them—and open those at the ankles as well, not on the same day; Petit, Wigan, and Ermerins are all agreed, that the negative particle, although wanting in the mss., is here required by the sense.for an interval is better both for a copious flow of blood and for restoring strength. One must draw off blood frequently and copiously, as it is the nourishment of the affection, while little in it is good—the nourishment of nature. Judge carefully, then, drawing off the bad blood and introducing proper nourishment in the interval, until the disease gives way from lack of nourishment; for the fresh blood, becoming interwoven with the body, over a long time effaces the old. Next give the hiera to drink, not just once, but let everything be repeated frequently after intervals of recovery. Let there also be the other medicinal purging in food—that for sciatica which I described—and undiluted milk in large quantity to drink for loosening the bowels, mixed with a fifth part of water so that all the milk may pass through. Bring the patient swiftly to emetics: first fasting, next after meals, then with radishes; let all be done frequently and continuously. Lead on to hellebore at every season, especially in spring and autumn, giving it
day after day and again in the following year. And if the disease is firmly established, give whatever medicinal drinks one knows, for it is good to medicate abundantly for benefit. I too shall write down what I know: mix one cyathus of cedar-oil with two of cabbage juice and administer; another: one cyathus of ironwort juice, one of trefoil, and two cyathi of wine and honey; another: one drachm by weight of ivory filings with two cyathi of Cretan wine. The flesh of vipers—the creeping beasts—molded into lozenges is also drunk: cut off about four fingers' breadth from both the head and the tail of each, boil the remainder until the bones separate, mold the flesh into lozenges, and dry them in the shade; administer these in drink just like squill. Vipers themselves may also be eaten as a dish at dinner, prepared like fish; and if the compound theriac of vipers is at hand, give it to drink instead of everything else, for it contains all ingredients together. Cleanse the body as well and smooth down the tubercles. Countless other remedies of the Celts, who are now called Gauls—those artificial alkaline balls with which they wash linen, called soap—are best for cleansing the body in the bath; purslane and houseleek with vinegar, and a decoction of dock roots with native sulfur, also cleanse well. A compound cleanser: smooth halcyonium, nitre, burnt vinegar lees, split alum, native sulfur, costus, iris, and pepper—mix all these, each according to its strength or in equal parts, sprinkle it on, and rub the body. For the tubercles of the face, mix ashes of vine-twigs with the fat of some wild animal—lion, panther, bear, or failing these, Egyptian goose (for like in unlike, like an ape to a man, is best)—and anoint; also gum ammoniac with vinegar and plantain or knotgrass juice, hypocist, and lycium.
If the flesh is livid, scarify beforehand to draw out the humors; if you wish to soothe parts excoriated by acrid discharges, a decoction of fenugreek or barley-gruel is a gentle cleanser, and rose or mastic oil for anointing. Frequent baths are beneficial to moisten and disperse the bad humors.

Let the food be clean, wholesome, digestible, and plain, and the regimen well ordered in every respect—sleep, walks, and places of residence; exercises such as running, rolling, and punching the leather bag, all without fatigue and with well-regulated exertion; let there also be vocal exercise, the proper exercise of the breath. Let the clothing be clean, not merely for appearance, but because soiled garments irritate the skin. Give wormwood wine to drink fasting; for breakfast, barley bread, seasoned pickled fish, and a little half-boiled mallow or cabbage with cumin sauce; for dinner, carrot root, groats with an old mixture of wine and honey, and seafood that loosens the bowels—broths of tellins, oysters, sea-urchins, and rock-fish; of land animals, wild game such as hare or boar; of birds, all partridges, wood-pigeons, rock-doves, and whatever the region produces best; seasonable orchard fruits; sweet wines are better than dry ones. Natural hot sulfurous baths, long residence at mineral waters, the sea, and sea voyages.

Helleborism: white hellebore is a purge of the upper belly, black hellebore of the lower. White hellebore is not merely an emetic, but the most powerful of all purges combined—not by the quantity and variety of the evacuation (for cholera does that too), nor by the straining and violence of the vomiting (for seasickness and the sea are stronger in that), but by a potency and quality of no mean order, by which it restores the sick to health even with a small evacuation and slight straining. Indeed, for all chronic diseases
rooted to their depths, when all other remedies have failed, this alone is a cure. For white hellebore resembles fire in its power; and whatever fire accomplishes by burning away, hellebore does even more by penetrating within—producing easy breathing out of dyspnea, good color out of pallor, and plump flesh out of emaciation.
